\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across six models (7B to 32B parameters), four reasoning domains, and over 2,400 instances with three-seed replication. Grounded in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, our analysis explains why Self-Consistency majority voting saturates and why symbolic constraint aggregation fails to break this plateau under same-model self-extraction.

The central finding is the independence bottleneck. Same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa$ values of $0.20$--$0.91$, and the effective sample size compresses to Eff-$K = 1.09$--$3.76$ at $K = 12$. Self-extracted FOL constraints inherit this correlation structure. SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone of approximately 50--55\% SC accuracy, where Mistral-7B on FOLIO achieves $+4.90$\,pp ($p = 0.013$, significant in 2 of 3 seeds). Outside this zone, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A) or error amplification actively degrades accuracy by $-2.83$\,pp (Type~C).

Oracle controls confirm that the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 35\% of this ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The uniform failure confirms the bottleneck is structural rather than an engineering artifact. Sensitivity analysis reinforces this conclusion: $K = 12$ marks the inverted-U peak, and the effect collapses at both $T = 0.3$ and $T = 1.0$.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost deployment diagnostic for predicting when symbolic aggregation can help. Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence as CJT requires: trained extractors, external provers, and multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation is limited to same-model self-extraction. We do not test trained FOL extractors, external solvers with verified grounding, or multi-model constraint pipelines, all of which may overcome the independence bottleneck.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The oracle experiments provide a causal identification of the failure source.
Holding all pipeline components fixed and varying only the constraint source, gold annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$; \S\ref{sec:oracle}).
Self-extraction captures only 34.5\% of this ceiling.
Because the aggregation mechanism is identical in both conditions, the gap between oracle and self-extracted performance localizes entirely to extraction quality, not to solver limitations or the MAX-SAT formulation.
The aggregation mechanism is sound; the constraints are not.

The Condorcet Jury Theorem predicts that aggregation improves accuracy only when voters contribute independent information \citep{condorcet1785, ladha1992correlated}.
Eff-$K < 2$ for most conditions (Table~\ref{tab:independence}) confirms that same-model traces violate this requirement at $K = 12$.
Symbolic constraints, despite their formal appearance, do not escape this bound.
The extraction step maps natural language traces to FOL through the same model distribution, so constraints inherit the correlation structure of the traces that produced them.
Even symbolic representations, which appear to introduce a qualitatively different signal (formal logic rather than natural language votes), collapse back into the shared model distribution once the extraction is performed by the same model.
The independence bottleneck is not about symbolic reasoning as a formalism; it is about self-extraction being unable to introduce information that the model does not already encode in its traces.

Nine interventions spanning six dimensions all fail to widen the Goldilocks zone (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
Contrastive prompting reduces the non-discriminative rate from 8.2\% to 6.0\%, but the newly discriminative constraints still mirror model bias.
Cross-model extraction produces 0\% discriminative constraints.
Temperature variations in both directions fail: lowering to $T = 0.3$ yields $\Delta = -0.49$\,pp (too correlated), and raising to $T = 1.0$ yields $\Delta = +0.49$\,pp (too noisy).
Even in-context learning with gold FOL examples ($\Delta = +0.50$\,pp, n.s.) cannot break the confirmation bias pattern.
The consistent failure across orthogonal intervention strategies constitutes the strongest evidence that the bottleneck is structural, not an artifact of prompt design or solver configuration.
If any single dimension had succeeded, the bottleneck could be attributed to engineering; the uniform failure across all six implicates the self-extraction paradigm itself.

Published systems that report positive results on logical reasoning each bypass same-model self-extraction.
DyLoS \citep{xu2026dylos} composes specialized solvers, Aristotle \citep{li2025aristotle} applies logic-complete decomposition, FoVer \citep{wang2025fover} trains dedicated FOL verifiers, and Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm} routes problems to external provers.
Our oracle result is consistent with their success: when constraints are discriminative (by whatever mechanism), symbolic aggregation works.
The critical difference is the source of constraints, not the aggregation procedure.
These systems trade the simplicity of self-extraction for architectures that introduce genuinely independent signal, exactly the property that CJT requires \citep{ladha1992correlated}.

For practitioners, $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate) combined with SC accuracy forms a zero-cost deployment diagnostic before any constraint extraction is attempted.
When $C_0 < 5\%$, SICA reduces to SC by construction (degenerate).
When SC exceeds ${\sim}60\%$, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A).
When SC falls below ${\sim}40\%$, error amplification makes constraints actively harmful (Type~C).
Only the narrow band around 50--55\% SC is favorable, and even there, self-extraction captures barely a third of the oracle ceiling.
Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence, as CJT predicts is necessary: trained extractors (data-driven), external provers (tool-augmented), and multi-model pipelines (ensemble-based).
Each introduces a constraint source that is not a deterministic function of the reasoning model's own distribution.

All six dimensions fail. The independence bottleneck is structural: it cannot be resolved by prompt engineering, solver refinements, or diversity manipulations within the same-model self-extraction paradigm.

lines: Trained verifiers offer a data-driven alternative to self-extraction. Outcome reward models (ORMs) score complete solutions \citep{cobbe2021gsm8k}, process reward models (PRMs) assign step-level scores and outperform outcome-level verification \citep{lightman2024prm}, and Math-Shepherd automates process supervision without human annotations \citep{wang2024mathshepherd}. Multi-agent debate refines answers through iterative natural-language discussion \citep{liang2023encouraging,du2023improving}, a paradigm distinct from SICA's one-shot symbolic aggregation. Self-correction methods attempt refinement without external feedback \citep{huang2024selfcorrect,madaan2023selfrefine}, but \citet{stechly2025selfverification} show that LLM self-verification degrades performance while sound external verification yields gains. Their finding parallels our capability trap in the high-accuracy regime. Both trained verifiers and SICA face extraction-quality challenges, but trained approaches may prove more robust because they learn discriminative patterns from data rather than relying on the same model's symbolic capabilities. The consistent pattern across this literature is that reliably improving on majority voting requires information beyond the reasoning model's own outputs (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
\paragraph{Condorcet Jury Theorem and Ensemble Diversity.}

-The Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785} establishes that majority voting among independent voters, each correct with probability $p > 0.5$, converges to correctness as the number of voters grows. \citet{austensmith1996} extend this result to information aggregation under strategic conditions. \citet{ladha1992correlated} prove that correlated voters reduce the effective ensemble size, a result we operationalize as $K_{\text{eff}} = K / (1 + (K{-}1) \cdot \kappa)$ in \S\ref{sec:condorcet}. \citet{lefort2024condorcet_llm} apply the CJT framework to LLM ensemble sentiment classification and document independence violations when all ensemble members share the same architecture. We extend this line of work to reasoning-trace aggregation, measuring $\kappa$ and $K_{\text{eff}}$ across 13 model-dataset conditions (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}). Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa} serves as our inter-rater agreement metric, connecting the voting-theory framework to a concrete diagnostic for when symbolic aggregation can improve over majority voting.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across six models (7B to 32B parameters), four reasoning domains, and over 2,400 instances with three-seed replication. Grounded in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, our analysis explains why Self-Consistency majority voting saturates and why symbolic constraint aggregation fails to break this plateau under same-model self-extraction.

The central finding is the independence bottleneck. Same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa$ values of $0.20$--$0.91$, and the effective sample size compresses to Eff-$K = 1.09$--$3.76$ at $K = 12$. Self-extracted FOL constraints inherit this correlation structure. SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone of approximately 50--55\% SC accuracy, where Mistral-7B on FOLIO achieves $+4.90$\,pp ($p = 0.013$, significant in 2 of 3 seeds). Outside this zone, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A) or error amplification actively degrades accuracy by $-2.83$\,pp (Type~C).

Oracle controls confirm that the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 35\% of this ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The uniform failure confirms the bottleneck is structural rather than an engineering artifact. Sensitivity analysis reinforces this conclusion: $K = 12$ marks the inverted-U peak for trace count, and only 1 of 4 temperature settings ($T = 0.7$) produces a significant effect.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost deployment diagnostic for predicting when symbolic aggregation can help. Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence as CJT requires: trained extractors, external provers, and multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation is limited to same-model self-extraction. We do not test trained FOL extractors, external solvers with verified grounding, or multi-model constraint pipelines, all of which may overcome the independence bottleneck.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across six models (7B to 32B parameters), four reasoning domains, and over 2,400 instances with three-seed replication. Grounded in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, our analysis explains why Self-Consistency majority voting saturates and why symbolic constraint aggregation fails to break this plateau under same-model self-extraction.

The central finding is the independence bottleneck. Same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa$ values of $0.20$--$0.91$, and the effective sample size compresses to Eff-$K = 1.09$--$3.76$ at $K = 12$. Self-extracted FOL constraints inherit this correlation structure. SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone of approximately 50--55\% SC accuracy, where Mistral-7B on FOLIO achieves $+4.90$\,pp ($p = 0.013$, significant in 2 of 3 seeds). Outside this zone, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A) or error amplification actively degrades accuracy by $-2.83$\,pp (Type~C).

Oracle controls confirm that the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 35\% of this ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The uniform failure confirms the bottleneck is structural rather than an engineering artifact. Sensitivity analysis reinforces this conclusion: $K = 12$ is the only setting with a significant positive effect among five $K$ values, and only 1 of 4 temperature settings ($T = 0.7$) produces a significant effect; both peaks coincide with the lowest SC baseline.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost deployment diagnostic for predicting when symbolic aggregation can help. Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence as CJT requires: trained extractors, external provers, and multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation is limited to same-model self-extraction. We do not test trained FOL extractors, external solvers with verified grounding, or multi-model constraint pipelines, all of which may overcome the independence bottleneck.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across six models (7B to 32B parameters), three reasoning domains (FOLIO, ProofWriter, LogiQA), and over 2,400 evaluation instances with three-seed replication. Grounded in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, our analysis explains why Self-Consistency majority voting saturates and why symbolic constraint aggregation fails to break this plateau under same-model self-extraction.

The central finding is the independence bottleneck. Same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa$ values of $0.20$--$0.91$, and the effective sample size compresses to Eff-$K = 1.09$--$3.76$ at $K = 12$. Self-extracted FOL constraints inherit this correlation structure. SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone of approximately 50--55\% SC accuracy, where Mistral-7B on FOLIO achieves $+4.90$\,pp ($p = 0.013$, significant in 2 of 3 seeds). Outside this zone, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A) or error amplification actively degrades accuracy by $-2.83$\,pp (Type~C).

Oracle controls confirm that the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 35\% of this ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The uniform failure confirms the bottleneck is structural rather than an engineering artifact. Sensitivity analysis reinforces this conclusion: $K = 12$ is the only setting with a significant positive effect among five $K$ values, and only 1 of 4 temperature settings ($T = 0.7$) produces a significant effect; both peaks coincide with the lowest SC baseline.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost deployment diagnostic for predicting when symbolic aggregation can help. Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence as CJT requires: trained extractors, external provers, and multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation is limited to same-model self-extraction. We do not test trained FOL extractors, external solvers with verified grounding, or multi-model constraint pipelines, all of which may overcome the independence bottleneck.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time computation scaling through multiple reasoning samples has emerged as a practical alternative to scaling model parameters \citep{snell2025scaling, guo2025deepseekr1}.
The dominant aggregation strategy, Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, samples $K$ chain-of-thought traces and selects the majority answer.
SC is simple, model-agnostic, and effective across tasks without additional training.
It is also hitting a ceiling.
\citet{loo2025reevaluating} demonstrate that gains from increasing $K$ plateau and even decline for strong models, a pattern consistent across model families and reasoning tasks.
The plateau is consequential: test-time compute is the primary knob available to practitioners who cannot retrain or scale model parameters, and if additional samples stop helping, aggregation-based scaling faces a hard limit.
The gap between SC's theoretical promise (independent correct voters converge to truth) and its practical behavior (saturating gains) points to a structural mismatch between the independence assumption underlying majority voting and the correlated nature of same-model traces.

Confidence-weighted \citep{taubenfeld2025cisc} and universal \citep{chen2024usc} extensions of SC alleviate this to a degree, but the core limitation persists.
Traces sampled from the same model carry correlated errors.
When most traces converge on the same (possibly wrong) answer, additional samples provide no new information, and majority voting has no mechanism to correct the shared bias.
Trained reward models \citep{lightman2024prm, wang2024mathshepherd} and diversity-aware sampling \citep{diverseaware2026} break this plateau by injecting external signal or controlling trace diversity, but require either trained verifiers or modifications to the sampling procedure.
A more fundamental question remains: can \emph{structured aggregation} over symbolic representations extract information from the same traces that majority voting cannot?
If symbolic representations capture logical relationships that natural language answers discard, aggregation over constraints could in principle recover signal that vote counting misses.

Recent neuro-symbolic methods suggest that formal reasoning can complement LLM generation.
Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm} and LINC \citep{olausson2023linc} translate natural language problems into first-order logic (FOL) for external provers.
More recent systems route problems to specialized solver paradigms \citep{xu2026dylos}, apply logic-complete decomposition \citep{li2025aristotle}, train dedicated FOL verifiers \citep{wang2025fover}, or employ multi-perspective grounding \citep{luo2025logicagent}.
These methods report gains on logical reasoning benchmarks, but each introduces components beyond the reasoning model itself: trained verifiers, multi-paradigm solver selection, or external knowledge bases.
A simpler question precedes these architectural extensions: can the \emph{same} model that generates reasoning traces also extract useful formal constraints from them?
If so, self-extraction would be a zero-cost upgrade to SC that requires no additional model, no training data, and no external prover.
Any LLM could be augmented with symbolic verification through a single extraction prompt and a satisfiability solver.
The appeal is practical: self-extraction scales with the base model, requires no domain-specific engineering, and preserves the simplicity that makes SC attractive in the first place.
Yet no prior work has systematically evaluated whether self-extracted constraints are useful for aggregation, or characterized the conditions under which they succeed or fail.
This question motivates our study of Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).

We ground our analysis in the Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785}, which provides a formal lens for understanding when aggregation succeeds.
CJT states that if $K$ independent voters each answer correctly with probability $p > 0.5$, the majority is correct with probability approaching 1 as $K$ grows \citep{austensmith1996}.
SC implicitly depends on this guarantee: when independence holds, more traces monotonically improve accuracy.
When it fails, as \citet{ladha1992correlated} show for correlated voters, additional samples carry diminishing information.
Same-model traces violate independence.
We measure inter-trace agreement with Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa} and find values from 0.20 to 0.91 across our experimental conditions, yielding an effective sample size (Eff-$K$) of 1.09 to 3.76 for nominal $K = 12$ (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
In practical terms, 12 sampled traces from the same model carry the information of fewer than 4 independent opinions, and in the most correlated conditions, barely more than 1.
At Eff-$K \approx 1$, each additional trace is informationally redundant, and no aggregation method operating on those traces alone can escape the plateau.
Symbolic verification could in principle inject independent signal, because formal logic validity does not depend on the generative model.
But when the same model both produces the reasoning trace and extracts the formal constraint, the constraint inherits the trace's biases and errors \citep{huang2024selfcorrect, kambhampati2024position}.
Self-extracted constraints do not constitute an independent check; they are a reformulation of the same evidence.
We term this the \emph{independence bottleneck}: the traces that produce constraints also determine their quality, so the constraints cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires for aggregation to surpass SC.
Recent work has examined CJT violations in LLM ensembles \citep{lefort2024condorcet_llm}, but no prior study connects this theoretical framework to symbolic constraint extraction.
The distinction matters: symbolic constraints appear to introduce a qualitatively different information source (formal logic rather than natural language votes), yet our analysis shows that the extraction step collapses this apparent independence back into the shared model distribution.

We evaluate SICA across six models (7B to 32B parameters), four reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}, StrategyQA \citep{geva2021strategyqa}), and more than 2,400 evaluation instances with three-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
Our evaluation spans instruction-tuned and reasoning-specialized model variants to ensure the findings are not artifacts of a single model family.
The core finding is that SICA effectiveness is regime-dependent, confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone of approximately 50--55\% SC accuracy.
Within this zone, Mistral-7B achieves $+4.90$\,pp on FOLIO ($p = 0.013$, significant in 2 of 3 seeds).
Outside it, three distinct failure modes emerge (\S\ref{sec:failure-modes}).
In Type~A conditions (SC $\geq$ 60\%), constraints exhibit confirmation bias and merely echo the majority answer; SICA provides no significant gain across all tested conditions ($N > 1{,}600$ combined).
In Type~C conditions (SC $\leq$ 40\%), predominantly incorrect traces produce noisy constraints that actively degrade accuracy ($-2.83$\,pp, $p < 0.01$).
In Type~B conditions, domains that resist formalization yield no useful signal regardless of model accuracy.

Oracle controls causally localize the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
Replacing self-extracted constraints with gold FOL annotations produces $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), proving the aggregation mechanism is sound when constraints are discriminative.
Self-extraction captures only 35\% of this oracle ceiling; the gap localizes to extraction quality, not solver limitations.
We test nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions (prompting, architecture, capability, verification, diversity, and filtering), and all fail to widen the Goldilocks zone (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
The bottleneck is structural: it cannot be resolved within the same-model self-extraction paradigm.
Sensitivity analysis provides further diagnostic evidence: SICA gain peaks sharply at $K = 12$ (the only setting with $\Delta > 2$\,pp among five $K$ values) and at $T = 0.7$ (the only significant result among four temperatures). In both cases, the peak coincides with the lowest SC baseline, suggesting that the underlying driver is the SC-level regime, not the hyperparameter itself (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
These patterns confirm that SICA's benefit is fragile, dependent on a precise balance of trace diversity and extraction quality that same-model sampling rarely achieves.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Independence Bottleneck.} We formalize the SC plateau through the Condorcet Jury Theorem. Same-model traces yield Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.20$--$0.91$ (Eff-$K = 1.09$--$3.76$ for $K = 12$), quantifying why additional traces provide diminishing returns. Self-extracted symbolic constraints inherit this correlation and cannot supply independent signal (\S\ref{sec:condorcet}, \S\ref{sec:effective-k}).

\item \textbf{Oracle-Extraction Gap.} Oracle constraints yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$), proving the aggregation mechanism is sound. Self-extraction captures only 35\% of this ceiling. The failure localizes to extraction quality, not the symbolic approach (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).

\item \textbf{Regime-Dependent Effect.} SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone ($\sim$50--55\% SC accuracy). Above this range, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative. Below it, error amplification degrades accuracy. Three failure modes (Type~A, B, C) explain the regime boundaries (\S\ref{sec:main-results}, \S\ref{sec:failure-modes}).

\item \textbf{Structural Bottleneck Diagnosis.} Nine remediation strategies spanning prompting, architecture, capability, verification, diversity, and filtering all fail to widen the effective zone, confirming the independence bottleneck is inherent to same-model self-extraction. $K$/temperature sensitivity analysis and entropy-conditioned breakdowns provide practitioners with deployment diagnostics for predicting when symbolic aggregation can and cannot help (\S\ref{sec:remediation}, \S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The oracle experiments provide a causal identification of the failure source.
Holding all pipeline components fixed and varying only the constraint source, gold annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$; \S\ref{sec:oracle}).
Self-extraction captures only 34.5\% of this ceiling.
Because the aggregation mechanism is identical in both conditions, the gap between oracle and self-extracted performance localizes entirely to extraction quality, not to solver limitations or the MAX-SAT formulation.
The aggregation mechanism is sound; the constraints are not.

The Condorcet Jury Theorem predicts that aggregation improves accuracy only when voters contribute independent information \citep{condorcet1785, ladha1992correlated}.
Eff-$K < 2$ for most conditions (Table~\ref{tab:independence}) confirms that same-model traces violate this requirement at $K = 12$.
Symbolic constraints, despite their formal appearance, do not escape this bound.
The extraction step maps natural language traces to FOL through the same model distribution, so constraints inherit the correlation structure of the traces that produced them.
Even symbolic representations, which appear to introduce a qualitatively different signal (formal logic rather than natural language votes), collapse back into the shared model distribution once the extraction is performed by the same model.
The independence bottleneck is not about symbolic reasoning as a formalism; it is about self-extraction being unable to introduce information that the model does not already encode in its traces.

Nine interventions spanning six dimensions all fail to widen the Goldilocks zone (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
Contrastive prompting reduces the non-discriminative rate from 8.2\% to 6.0\%, but the newly discriminative constraints still mirror model bias.
Cross-model extraction produces 0\% discriminative constraints.
Only 1 of 4 temperature settings produces a significant SICA effect; $T = 0.3$, $0.5$, and $1.0$ all yield $|\Delta| \leq 0.49$\,pp.
Even in-context learning with gold FOL examples ($\Delta = +0.50$\,pp, n.s.) cannot break the confirmation bias pattern.
The consistent failure across orthogonal intervention strategies constitutes the strongest evidence that the bottleneck is structural, not an artifact of prompt design or solver configuration.
If any single dimension had succeeded, the bottleneck could be attributed to engineering; the uniform failure across all six implicates the self-extraction paradigm itself.

Published systems that report positive results on logical reasoning each bypass same-model self-extraction.
DyLoS \citep{xu2026dylos} composes specialized solvers, Aristotle \citep{li2025aristotle} applies logic-complete decomposition, FoVer \citep{wang2025fover} trains dedicated FOL verifiers, and Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm} routes problems to external provers.
Our oracle result is consistent with their success: when constraints are discriminative (by whatever mechanism), symbolic aggregation works.
The critical difference is the source of constraints, not the aggregation procedure.
These systems trade the simplicity of self-extraction for architectures that introduce genuinely independent signal, exactly the property that CJT requires \citep{ladha1992correlated}.

For practitioners, $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate) combined with SC accuracy forms a zero-cost deployment diagnostic before any constraint extraction is attempted.
When $C_0 < 5\%$, SICA reduces to SC by construction (degenerate).
When SC exceeds ${\sim}60\%$, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A).
When SC falls below ${\sim}40\%$, error amplification makes constraints actively harmful (Type~C).
Only the narrow band around 50--55\% SC is favorable, and even there, self-extraction captures barely a third of the oracle ceiling.
Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence, as CJT predicts is necessary: trained extractors (data-driven), external provers (tool-augmented), and multi-model pipelines (ensemble-based).
Each introduces a constraint source that is not a deterministic function of the reasoning model's own distribution.

148	\section{Z3 MaxSAT Evaluation Pseudocode}
149	\label{app:z3-pseudocode}
150	
151	Algorithm~\ref{alg:maxsat} describes the Z3 MaxSAT solving procedure. Algorithm~\ref{alg:scorer} describes the source-trace attribution scoring.
152	
153	Domain constraint variables (e.g., \texttt{x + y == 14}) and answer assertion variables (e.g., \texttt{\_\_sica\_answer\_42 == True}) are logically independent in the Z3 formulation. Discriminative signal arises solely from conflicts among domain constraints: when traces supporting different answers produce mutually contradictory constraints, the solver excludes the lower-weight subset, and the scorer penalizes the corresponding answers.
154	
155	\begin{algorithm}[h]
156	\caption{Z3 Weighted Partial MAX-SAT}
157	\label{alg:maxsat}
158	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
159	\Require Deduplicated constraint set $\mathcal{C} = \{(c_m, w_m, S_m)\}_{m=1}^M$ where $c_m$ is a Z3 formula, $w_m$ is weight, $S_m$ is the set of source trace indices
160	\Ensure Partition $(\mathcal{C}^*, \mathcal{C}^{\setminus})$ where $\mathcal{C}^*$ is the max-weight satisfiable subset
161	\State $\textit{opt} \gets \textsc{Z3.Optimize()}$
162	\For{$m = 1, \ldots, M$}
163	    \State $b_m \gets$ fresh Boolean indicator
164	    \State $\textit{opt}.\textsc{Add}(b_m \Rightarrow c_m)$ \Comment{soft clause guarded by indicator}
165	    \State $\textit{opt}.\textsc{AddSoft}(b_m,\; \text{weight}=w_m)$
166	\EndFor
167	\State $\textit{result} \gets \textit{opt}.\textsc{Check}()$
168	\State $\textit{model} \gets \textit{opt}.\textsc{Model}()$
169	\State $\mathcal{C}^* \gets \{(c_m, w_m, S_m) : \textit{model}(b_m) = \top\}$
170	\State $\mathcal{C}^{\setminus} \gets \mathcal{C} \setminus \mathcal{C}^*$
171	\State \Return $(\mathcal{C}^*, \mathcal{C}^{\setminus})$
172	\end{algorithmic}
173	\end{algorithm}
174	
175	\begin{algorithm}[h]
176	\caption{Source-Trace Attribution Scoring}
177	\label{alg:scorer}
178	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
179	\Require Satisfied set $\mathcal{C}^*$, excluded set $\mathcal{C}^{\setminus}$, candidate answers $\mathcal{A}$, trace-answer mapping $\tau: \text{trace\_idx} \to a$, penalty weight $\alpha$
180	\Ensure Score $s(a)$ for each $a \in \mathcal{A}$
181	\For{each $a \in \mathcal{A}$}
182	    \State $T_a \gets \{i : \tau(i) = a\}$ \Comment{trace indices producing answer $a$}
183	    \State $\textit{pos}(a) \gets \sum_{(c,w,S) \in \mathcal{C}^*} w \cdot \mathbf{1}[S \cap T_a \neq \emptyset]$
184	    \State $\textit{neg}(a) \gets \sum_{(c,w,S) \in \mathcal{C}^{\setminus}} w \cdot \mathbf{1}[S \cap T_a \neq \emptyset]$
185	    \State $s(a) \gets \textit{pos}(a) - \alpha \cdot \textit{neg}(a)$
186	\EndFor
187	\State \Return $a^* = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} s(a)$
188	\end{algorithmic}
189	\end{algorithm}

270	\section{Case Studies: Discordant Predictions}
271	\label{app:case-studies}
272	
273	Among 804 problems, SICA and SC agree on 773 (96.1\%). The 31 discordant cases comprise 16 SICA wins (SICA correct, SC wrong), 14 SC wins (SC correct, SICA wrong), and 1 where both select different wrong answers. All 31 occur at exact ties (entropy${=}1.0$, 6:6 vote split) or near-ties (entropy${\geq}0.9183$, 8:4 at most), since SICA can differ from SC only when constraint weights shift the majority away from SC's tiebreak choice. We present three representative cases that illustrate the mechanism behind capability trap failures.
274	
275	\paragraph{Case 1: SICA Wins (folio\_134, FOLIO).}
276	
277	\emph{Premises}: Some mammals have teeth. Platypus have no teeth. Platypus are mammals. Humans have teeth. \emph{Conclusion}: Humans are mammals. \emph{Gold}: Unknown.
278	
279	The premises state that \emph{some} mammals have teeth and that humans have teeth, but ``having teeth'' is not sufficient for ``being a mammal'' under open-world semantics. SC produces a 6:6 split (Unknown:6, True:6) and tiebreaks alphabetically to True (wrong). SICA extracts 7 constraints; MaxSAT excludes 1 constraint inconsistent with the rest, reducing the weighted score for True-voting traces and tipping the aggregation to Unknown (correct). The excluded constraint likely captured an incorrect inference step (e.g., affirming the consequent) present only in True-voting traces. While SICA succeeds here, the success is coincidental: the excluded constraint happens to anti-correlate with the correct answer.
280	
281	\paragraph{Case 2: SC Wins (ProofWriter-1066\_Q6, ProofWriter).}
282	
283	\emph{Key chain}: White(Bob)$\to$Round(Bob) [white things are round] $\to$ Young(Bob) [all round things are young]. \emph{Conclusion}: ``Bob is not young.'' \emph{Gold}: False (Bob IS young).
284	
285	SC produces a 6:6 split (False:6, True:6) and tiebreaks to False (correct). SICA extracts 17 constraints; MaxSAT excludes 2 that appear preferentially in False-voting traces. These excluded constraints likely captured correct intermediate derivations (e.g., \texttt{young\_bob == True}) that appeared only in traces completing the full deduction chain. By excluding them, MaxSAT removes evidence supporting the correct answer. SICA selects True (wrong). This case illustrates how self-extracted constraints can systematically mislead: correct reasoning steps become discriminative signals that the solver mistakenly penalizes.
286	
287	\paragraph{Case 3: Non-discriminative Constraints (ProofWriter-903\_Q6, ProofWriter).}
288	
289	\emph{Key chain}: Nice(Mouse)$\to$Cold(Mouse) [all nice people are cold] $\to$ Chases(Mouse,Mouse) [nice and cold $\to$ chase mouse]. \emph{Conclusion}: ``The mouse does not chase the mouse.'' \emph{Gold}: False.
290	
291	SC produces a 6:6 split (False:6, Unknown:6) and tiebreaks to False (correct). SICA extracts 44 constraints but excludes only 1 (2.3\%). The remaining 43 are domain facts and grounded rules (\texttt{nice\_mouse == True}, \texttt{Implies(nice\_mouse, cold\_mouse)}, etc.) that Z3 satisfies identically regardless of the final answer. Both False-voting and Unknown-voting traces share the same premises and grounded rules; they differ only in whether the trace completed the full derivation chain. The single excluded constraint carries negligible weight against 43 shared constraints, so SICA collapses to SC.
292

314	\section{ProofWriter Oracle Per-Subtype Analysis}
315	\label{app:pw-oracle-subtype}
316	
317	ProofWriter problems encode deductive rules as Domain-Specific Language (DSL) logic programs. Each problem uses one of four predicate subtypes: attribute predicates with or without negation (AttNeg, AttNoneg), and relation predicates with or without negation (RelNeg, RelNoneg). Relation predicates involve binary relations between entities (e.g., \texttt{eats(bear, squirrel)}), while attribute predicates assign unary properties (e.g., \texttt{kind(anne)}).
318	
319	The oracle pipeline parses these DSL annotations deterministically into Z3 formulas without any LLM involvement. Of the 600 ProofWriter problems, 594 (99.0\%) produce valid Z3 parses; the remaining 6 fail due to unsupported DSL constructs. Across all 7{,}128 trace-problem pairs submitted to Z3, the solver returns a result in every case (0\% solver errors). Z3 evaluations agree with ground-truth labels on 577 of 594 parseable problems (97.14\%), confirming that the deterministic DSL-to-Z3 translation faithfully preserves problem semantics.
320	
321	Table~\ref{tab:pw_oracle_subtype} reports the per-subtype breakdown. Relation-predicate subtypes show substantially larger gains than attribute-predicate subtypes: RelNeg improves by $+17.86$~pp and RelNoneg by $+13.01$~pp, compared to $+9.09$~pp for AttNoneg and $+6.87$~pp for AttNeg. Relation predicates involve longer reasoning chains with more intermediate entities, producing greater answer diversity across traces ($C_0$) and more opportunities for oracle constraints to correct errors.
